title: DeepSeek-R1 dialogue leads a 34-year-old man to a genetically confirmed familial Mediterranean fever diagnosis after roughly three decades of symptoms
summary: A patient's dialogue with DeepSeek-R1-0528 pointed to familial Mediterranean fever, genetic testing confirmed it, and colchicine stopped attacks after ~30 years of symptoms.
account: A 34-year-old man of Egyptian origin began a dialogue with the DeepSeek-R1-0528 model on 28 June 2025. He had recurrent fever, migratory abdominal pain, arthralgia, myalgia and erythematous skin lesions since early childhood. The model refined its differential toward familial Mediterranean fever (FMF). It recommended specialist evaluation, inflammatory markers, genetic testing and colchicine under supervision. He arranged genetic testing, which found two pathogenic MEFV variants (p.Met694Val and p.Val726Ala). He obtained colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily from an Egyptian pharmacy. His attacks ceased, but alanine aminotransferase rose to 160 U/L. Colchicine was temporarily discontinued, and his primary care physician monitored his liver enzymes. After they improved, colchicine was resumed at 0.5 mg daily under close supervision. In February 2026 he presented to the Department of Medicine III, University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, Germany, already taking 0.5 mg daily. The clinic confirmed FMF, and he has remained attack-free. The authors of the case report declare that they have no competing interests. In a study published on 31 October 2025, Selin Cilli Hayıroğlu and Tugce Bozkurt, rheumatologists in Istanbul, found that ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok answered diagnosis questions on FMF less well than other questions about the disease.
purpose: DeepSeek-R1 is a general-purpose reasoning chatbot. Answering a user's medical questions with a differential diagnosis falls within its general question-answering function. It is not a validated medical device.
segment: Patient-initiated use of a consumer LLM

ratings.reason: Inflammatory attacks that had recurred since early childhood ceased on colchicine after a genetically confirmed diagnosis. The benefit is life-changing, tempered by a documented transaminase rise from self-dosing before medical supervision.

ai_role.statement: The large language model (LLM) generated the FMF hypothesis and the suggested work-up over a multi-turn dialogue. Confirmation came from MEFV genotyping and clinical response to colchicine. The authors stress that the model repeatedly advised specialist supervision. The self-directed genetic testing and self-medication were the patient's own actions.

brief: A 34-year-old man of Egyptian origin had recurrent inflammatory attacks from early childhood, and despite almost three decades of symptoms, extensive investigations had not established a diagnosis. On 28 June 2025 he began a dialogue with the DeepSeek-R1-0528 model, which refined its differential diagnosis toward familial Mediterranean fever and repeatedly advised specialist supervision. He arranged genetic testing himself, and it showed two pathogenic MEFV variants. His attacks stopped on colchicine that he obtained from an Egyptian pharmacy and took on his own, but his liver enzymes rose and the drug was paused.[1] It was resumed at a lower dose under close supervision. In February 2026 he presented to the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, which confirmed the diagnosis, and he has remained free of attacks.[2] The model's part was the hypothesis and the suggested work-up; the confirmation came from genetic testing and his response to colchicine. The evidence for the benefit comes from one patient. In a study published on 31 October 2025, two rheumatologists in Istanbul found that ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok answered patient questions on familial Mediterranean fever best on recovery and follow-up and less well on diagnosis.[3]

display.answer: The case report by Pauz, Kremer, Xiong and Krusche is the only source for the patient's case. The record cites it twice, for two quotations. In their 2025 study, Cilli Hayıroğlu and Bozkurt report that two clinical experts rated answers from ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok to patient questions on familial Mediterranean fever. That study does not concern this patient.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: A patient's dialogue with DeepSeek-R1-0528 pointed to familial Mediterranean fever, genetic testing confirmed it, and colchicine stopped attacks after ~30 years of symptoms.
fields.account: A 34-year-old man of Egyptian origin began a dialogue with the DeepSeek-R1-0528 model on 28 June 2025. He had recurrent fever, migratory abdominal pain, arthralgia, myalgia and erythematous skin lesions since early childhood. The model refined its differential toward familial Mediterranean fever (FMF). It recommended specialist evaluation, inflammatory markers, genetic testing and colchicine under supervision. He arranged genetic testing, which found two pathogenic MEFV variants (p.Met694Val and p.Val726Ala). He obtained colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily from an Egyptian pharmacy. His attacks ceased, but alanine aminotransferase rose to 160 U/L. Colchicine was temporarily discontinued, and his primary care physician monitored his liver enzymes. After they improved, colchicine was resumed at 0.5 mg daily under close supervision. In February 2026 he presented to the Department of Medicine III, University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, Germany, already taking 0.5 mg daily. The clinic confirmed FMF, and he has remained attack-free. The authors of the case report declare that they have no competing interests. In a study published on 31 October 2025, Selin Cilli Hayıroğlu and Tugce Bozkurt, rheumatologists in Istanbul, found that ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok answered diagnosis questions on FMF less well than other questions about the disease.
